The Kalevala Is Published: Elias Lönnrot has walked the parish roads with his notebook, and out of a thousand singers' mouths he has stitched the old songs into one tale: Väinämöinen's wisdom, the forging of the Sampo, the doings of gods and heroes. The Kalevala lies printed in Helsinki, and every farmhouse that learns to read it learns also that the Finnish tongue has an epic of its own.
Let the songs be read in every parish!
A curiosity for the scholars.
The Language Strife

The business of the realm runs in Swedish, the pulpits and the schoolhouses run in Finnish. The fennomans demand that the language of the four Estates be the language of the state. The svecomans answer that Swedish law and Swedish learning built this land. The Diet must choose which tongue shall govern.
Finnish shall be the language of the land.
The old tongue of the law shall stand.
The Diet Assembles

For the first time in half a century the Estates of the realm are summoned to Porvoo: clergy, nobility, burghers and the farmers - the last an estate no other realm grants its peasantry. The Diet deliberates on currency, roads, schools, and the standing of the Finnish tongue.
Let the Estates meet and the realm prosper.
We shall govern without their advice.
The First Railway

Smoke and iron between Helsinki and Hämeenlinna: the first stretch of track in the land is open. The engineers have laid it to a gauge wider than the Russian one, so that no invader's rolling stock may ride it - a small decision, much remembered.
Widen the rails and bind the land together.
The Finnish Guard Battalion

A battalion of the line, recruited from Finnish soil and drilled in Helsinki, has won its colors. For the young men of the parish it is a school of arms - and of national feeling, the Guard's bandsmen play Finnish airs on parade days, and the crowd hums along.
The Guard marches under its own flag.
Keep the youth at their ploughs.
The Markka and the Bank

The Bank of Suomi shall issue a markka of its own, tied to silver, and the realm shall price its timber and tar in its own coin. The merchants of Helsinki and Turku toast the new banknotes, the ruble's agents take note.
Honest coin for an honest people.
The February Manifesto

A decree from Petersburg has swept away the Diet's old privileges by a stroke of the imperial pen. The officials call it administrative order, the lawyers call it usurpation. Across the land a strange silence follows - and beneath the silence, a petition with half a million names, and song meetings that are not quite political and not quite innocent.
We shall resist lawfully and without violence.
Submission, for now.
A National Music

A young composer has drawn the Kalevala's runs into music: the kantele's plucked strings and the deep drone of strings and brass, old tunes set for concert halls. Foreign critics call it northern fire, at home, everyone simply recognizes it.
Let the world hear what our forests sound like.
The Folk High Schools

On the Danish pattern, the movement has founded folk high schools: boarding houses of learning for grown farmers' sons and daughters, where history and the mother tongue are taught by lantern light in the winter months. The students return to their parishes reading newspapers and asking questions.
A school in every province!
The parish schools suffice.
The America Letters

From the iron mines of Michigan and the forests of Wisconsin the letters come back, in careful Finnish on ruled paper: wages beyond imagining, land for the taking, and cold winters that kill a man's homesickness. In the parish houses they are read aloud, and the young men look at the door.
Let those who must go, go - and send money home.
The land needs its strong arms here.
The Sea Fortress Refit

The old Swedish bastions on the islands before Helsinki have kept their silence for a century, modern shells would laugh at them. The engineers propose new batteries, casemates, and coastal guns. It is ruinously expensive, and the grand duchy's budget is not its own to spend.
Spare no expense on the guns.
A modest refit will do.
Kansakoulu: Schools for the People

A primary school law for the whole land: every child shall learn letters and numbers in the mother tongue, and the parish shall keep the schoolhouse. It will cost money and teachers, and it will return a people who cannot be told what to think, because they can read.
Every child, every parish, every year.
The Church already teaches the letters.
The Sauna Parliament

No statute decrees it, yet every traveler learns it: the true business of the countryside is settled in the steam. In the sauna the farmer and the neighbor speak as equals, grievances soften, and the village finds one mind. The foreign observer finds nothing to report, the census of well-being rises nonetheless.
Where the steam rises, the quarrels fall.
The Purge of the University

A new statute from Petersburg: the University's chairs shall answer to the imperial ministry, discipline committees shall root out seditious teaching, and history is to be instructed with the proper reverence for the empire's unity. Professors resign rather than sign, students boycott the lectures.
The scholars resist - quietly and completely.
We cannot shield them from the ministry.
The Underground Press

The gendarmes confiscate the printing press, a week later another one runs in a barn loft, printing on cheap paper with a hand-inked plate. The forbidden journal travels by boat and by schoolmistress's basket. Every seizure makes the next printing bolder.
Let the words travel by night.
Look away - we saw nothing.
